section.title: A Wedding Song for the King
section.sectionRationale: Titled 'a love song' in its superscription, this royal wedding psalm addresses the Davidic king in language so exalted, his throne is called God's own, verse 6, that the author of Hebrews applies it directly to Christ, Hebrews 1:8-9, making it one of the clearest messianic psalms in the Psalter.
section.thesis: This wedding song praises the ideal king, righteous, victorious, and anointed above his companions, in terms no merely human king could fully bear, terms the New Testament recognizes as belonging finally to Christ, the eternal King whose throne is forever and whose bride, the church, is called to undivided devotion.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the poet's inspired theme, verses 1-2; the summons to the warrior king, verses 3-5; the king's eternal, God-called throne and anointing, verses 6-9; the address to the bride, verses 10-15; and the promise of enduring dynasty and fame, verses 16-17.

units.label: My heart is stirred by a noble theme

verses.text:
My heart is stirred by a noble theme as I recite my verses to the king; 
my tongue is the pen of a skillful writer.

You are the most handsome of men; grace has anointed your lips, 
since God has blessed you forever.

units.label: Strap your sword at your side, O mighty warrior
units.note: the summons to the warrior king

verses.text: Strap your sword at your side, O mighty warrior; appear in your majesty and splendor.

In your splendor ride forth in victory on behalf of truth and humility and justice; 
may your right hand show your awesome deeds.
Your arrows pierce the hearts of the king's foes; the nations fall beneath your feet.

units.label: Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever
units.note: the king's eternal, God-called throne and anointing

verses.text: Your throne, O {{elohim|God}}, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom.
You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you above your companions with the oil of {{sasson|joy}}.

All your garments are fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia; 
from palaces of ivory the harps make you glad.

The daughters of kings are among your honored women; the queen stands at your right hand, 
adorned with the gold of Ophir.

units.label: Listen, O daughter, forget your people

verses.text: Listen, O daughter! Consider and incline your ear: Forget your people and your father's house,
and the king will desire your beauty; bow to him, for he is your lord.
The Daughter of Tyre will come with a gift; men of wealth will seek your favor.
All glorious is the princess in her chamber; her gown is embroidered with gold.
In colorful garments she is led to the king; her virgin companions are brought before you.
They are led in with joy and gladness; they enter the palace of the king.

units.label: I will commemorate your name through all generations
units.note: the promise of enduring dynasty and fame

verses.text: Your sons will succeed your fathers; you will make them princes throughout the land.
I will commemorate your name through all generations; therefore the nations will praise you forever and ever.

elohim.gloss: God. The psalmist astonishingly addresses the king's throne with this title, language no merely human king could rightly bear without qualification. The writer of Hebrews quotes this very line as the Father's own address to the Son, Hebrews 1:8.

sasson.gloss: Joy or gladness, especially festive joy. The king is anointed with this oil above his companions, language Hebrews 1:9 applies to Christ, anointed with the oil of gladness beyond His companions.

basic.context: Titled a love song, this psalm was composed for a royal wedding, praising the Davidic king's righteousness, victory, and splendor, then addressing his bride with counsel to leave her own people and cling wholly to him. Its language becomes so exalted, calling the king's throne God's own throne, that it points beyond any merely human king.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm functioned first as a real celebration for a historical royal wedding, yet its language so exceeds what any human king could bear on his own, especially verse 6, that Scripture itself, in Hebrews 1, reads it as ultimately fulfilled in Christ, the true and greater King.
basic.originalLanguages: The king's throne is called elohim, God, verse 6, astonishing language quoted directly by Hebrews as the Father's address to the Son. He is anointed with the oil of sasson, joy, above his companions, verse 7, language Hebrews 1:9 also applies to Christ's unique anointing above all others.
basic.typology: The king's eternal throne, called God's own, and his anointing above his companions with the oil of joy point forward to Christ, the true King whose throne is truly and eternally divine and whose anointing as Messiah exceeds every other. The bride summoned to leave her people for the king anticipates the church, the bride of Christ.
basic.christ: Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes Psalm 45:6-7 directly as words the Father speaks to the Son, proof of Christ's full deity and eternal reign. The whole psalm's picture of a righteous, victorious, radiant King wedded to a devoted bride finds its truest fulfillment in Christ and His church.
basic.god: God is shown anointing and establishing the king's throne, blessing him forever, and Himself being the one whose own throne the king's throne images, so that the king's righteous reign becomes a window onto God's own eternal, just kingship.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes this psalm directly as the Father's address to the Son. Ephesians 5:25-32 describes Christ's love for His bride, the church, in similarly devoted terms. Revelation 19:7-9 pictures the marriage supper of the Lamb, the wedding this psalm anticipates.
basic.oneStory: This royal wedding song, praising an anointed king whose throne is called God's own, points beyond any human king to Christ, the eternal King and Bridegroom, whose bride, the church, is called to forsake every lesser loyalty for undivided devotion to Him.

context.literary:
Psalm 45 is a song with a frame and two panels. The frame is the poet's voice in verse 1 and again in verse 17, where 'I' begins and ends the poem with the pen of a scribe and a promise to keep the king's name alive. Inside the frame the king is addressed in verses 2 to 9 and the bride in verses 10 to 15, and the last two verses turn back to the king and his line. The poem therefore runs king, bride, king, in the shape of a wedding procession that starts at the throne, pauses for the bride's instruction, and returns with descendants.

The king's panel has its own movement. Verse 2 praises his beauty and his lips, which are what a king needs to be seen and heard. Verses 3 to 5 call him to war, and the goals of the war are surprising: 'truth and humility and justice', verse 4. He is a warrior whose weapons serve righteousness. Verses 6 and 7 are the centre of the poem, moving from his throne to his character to his anointing, and everything before them prepares for them and everything after depends on them. Verses 8 and 9 then paint the court in scent and music.

The bride's panel is a piece of counsel. Four imperatives open it, 'Listen', 'Consider', 'incline your ear', 'Forget', and the counsel is followed by a promise, 'and the king will desire your beauty'. The second half of the panel is a description of the procession: the wealthy of Tyre come with gifts, the princess is glorious in her chamber, and the company is led in 'with joy and gladness' to the palace.

The poem's tone is deliberately elevated. Verse 1 tells us the poet's heart 'is stirred', a word for a bubbling up, and the whole psalm reads as praise that overflows. It also plays on the image of the pen. The king's lips are gracious, the poet's tongue is a pen, and the poem is a written monument to a spoken grace.
context.historical:
The heading gives the tune as 'Lilies', calls the psalm a maskil of the sons of Korah, and labels it a love song. It belongs to the court of a Davidic king and was presumably sung at a royal wedding. The details fit the wealth of the united monarchy or later. Ivory work and gold from Ophir mark the kind of luxury associated with Solomon: 1 Kings 9:28 has his fleet bringing gold from Ophir and 1 Kings 10:18 says he made a great throne of ivory overlaid with pure gold. Song of Songs 3:11 describes Solomon's wedding day. Other kings could equally have been the occasion, and the text does not name the groom or the bride.

The mention of the Daughter of Tyre, verse 12, reflects diplomatic ties. Solomon and Hiram of Tyre were allies, and royal marriages sealed treaties in the ancient Near East. A foreign princess would be expected to bring gifts, and the psalm has the wealthy of Tyre bring tribute. The queen who is told to forget her people and her father's house, verse 10, is therefore most naturally a foreign bride entering a new court. The words also recall Abram's call to leave his country and his father's household, Genesis 12:1, and Ruth's vow that Israel's people would be hers, Ruth 1:16.

The warrior imagery is standard for kings. A king's first duty was to defend the people and uphold justice, and the coronation psalms ask for both, Psalm 72:1-2. Psalm 45 shows a king in his glory, and it belongs to the family of royal psalms with Psalms 2, 72, 110 and 144.

There was also a darker history. Solomon's foreign wives turned his heart to other gods, 1 Kings 11:1-4. The psalm's counsel to the bride that she should forget her people and give herself wholly to the king takes on a bitter irony in that light. The earthly king fell short of the ideal, and the song outruns him.
context.canonical:
Psalm 45 is one of the pivotal psalms of the Psalter's royal theology. Psalm 2 presents the anointed king installed on Zion and addressed as God's Son, and Psalm 110 gives him a seat at the Lord's right hand. Psalm 72 asks God to endow the king with His justice. Psalm 45 shows the same king in the intimacy of his wedding. Together they build the picture that the Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7:12-16, a son whose throne will be established forever, is a promise of a person whose reign is just, victorious and joyful.

The key text is verses 6 and 7. Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes them in full as words the Father speaks to the Son: 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom.' The chapter is a chain of Old Testament quotations meant to show that the Son is greater than the angels, and Psalm 45 is used at the point where the Son is addressed as God. The BSB footnote to Psalm 45:7 records the citation.

The wedding imagery reaches through the prophets and into the New Testament. Isaiah 62:5 promises that God will rejoice over His people as a bridegroom over a bride. Hosea 2:19 has God betroth Israel to Himself forever. John the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom and himself the friend of the bridegroom, John 3:29. Jesus tells parables of a king who prepared a wedding banquet for his son, Matthew 22:2, and of virgins waiting for the bridegroom, Matthew 25:1. Paul speaks of presenting the church as a pure virgin to Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:2, and describes Christ's love for the church in Ephesians 5:25-27. The book of Revelation closes the sequence with the marriage of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7-9, and the new Jerusalem as a bride adorned for her husband, Revelation 21:2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet was a court singer writing for a specific occasion, and his first aim was to honour the king and bless the marriage. He is proud of his skill, as verse 1 shows, and he wants to speak well of the king and of the God who made him what he is. The heart of his praise is not beauty or wealth but the king's character: 'You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness'. He wants the court and the nation to see that the king's greatness rests on justice.

He also wants the king himself to hear the standard. The poem describes an ideal ruler in the language of praise, and praise of that sort was also a charge. To call the king a champion of truth, humility and justice is to tell him what a king is for. In the same way, the counsel to the bride sets out the loyalty that a royal marriage required.

At the same time, the poet's language reaches beyond what any king could carry. He calls the throne eternal and God's own, and he promises that the king's name will be remembered by all the nations forever. It is difficult to think that he meant these words as hollow flattery. A Davidic court that lived on the promise of 2 Samuel 7 would have heard them as the confidence that God's covenant would produce a king who fulfils them. The original hearers were meant to rejoice in the king they had and to look for the king the promise described.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a royal wedding and the praise offered to a king. It does not prescribe marriage customs, nor does it teach that any modern ruler is to be addressed in such terms. The bride's instruction to forget her father's house and to bow to her lord describes the expectation of an ancient court, and it should not be lifted out and made into a rule for how a husband and wife relate today. The New Testament takes up the marriage image and reshapes it: the husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, Ephesians 5:25, so the model of the greater bridegroom is sacrificial love.

The warrior king also needs care. The psalm celebrates a king who rides out in victory, but it names the causes as truth, humility and justice. It does not authorise violence in the name of religion. Where the New Testament applies the picture to Christ, He conquers by the word of His mouth and by His own death, and the church's part is to bear witness.

What carries forward is the truth about the king. The psalm teaches that the ruler God chooses is righteous, that his reign is anointed with joy, and that a people can trust him. It also teaches that those who belong to him give him first loyalty. That principle is picked up in the New Testament, and it is the one that applies to every believer.

debates.question: How should 'Your throne, O God' in verse 6 be understood?

views.label: The king is addressed as 'God'
views.case: The natural reading of the Hebrew is a direct address: 'Your throne, O God, endures forever.' Ancient Israel's kings were sometimes spoken of in exalted terms, as in Isaiah 9:6, where the promised child is called 'Mighty God'. Hebrews 1:8 takes the words as addressed to the Son and calls Him God. The BSB reads the verse this way.

views.label: 'Your throne is God's throne'
views.case: Some translators render the phrase 'Your throne is of God' or 'Your throne is God', taking the word for God as a description of the throne's source. The Hebrew allows it, and the reading avoids calling a human king God. It remains close to the meaning of the verse that the throne belongs to God as its giver.

views.label: An address to God about the king
views.case: A few take verse 6 as the poet turning to address God Himself. This creates a break in the flow, since verse 7 returns to speaking of the king, and it is a less common view.

debates.bearing: The direct address is the simplest reading and the one the writer to the Hebrews adopts. Even if a human king was in view, the poem's claim outruns him, which is why the church has read it as spoken to the Messiah.

debates.question: Is Psalm 45 about a historical king, or about the Messiah from the start?

views.label: A historical royal wedding
views.case: The heading, the setting in a court with a foreign princess, the names of Tyre and Ophir, and the request for sons all belong to a real occasion. On this view the New Testament reads the psalm in the light of Christ without denying its first setting.

views.label: Messianic from the beginning
views.case: The language of eternal throne and anointing is more than a court could bear, and the Davidic promise gave the poet reason to speak of a coming king. On this reading the psalm is a prophecy that uses a wedding as its frame.

views.label: A royal psalm with typological fullness
views.case: The psalm honours a real king, whose reign was a type of the greater one. The language is heightened because the office was meant to point beyond its holders. This is the most common view in the church's reading.

debates.bearing: The third view respects both the first occasion and the New Testament's use. The king was real, and his office was a promise still awaiting its full holder.

study.originalLanguages:
The lexicon word for 'joy' in verse 7 is sasson, the oil of gladness. It appears again in Isaiah 61:3, 'the oil of joy for mourning', where the Anointed One brings good news to the afflicted. The pairing of anointing oil with joy in both places makes Psalm 45:7 more than a description of a coronation; it points toward a king whose anointing brings gladness to others. The verb 'anointed' in the same verse is mashach, the root of Messiah, so the verse contains the word that gave the title to the promised King.

In verse 1 the poet says his tongue is 'the pen of a skillful writer'. The word for skilful, mahir, is used of Ezra, 'a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses', Ezra 7:6. It is a word for expertise that comes with practice. The poet claims to compose with a scribe's quick, sure hand, but he does so because his heart is stirred, a rare verb that suggests something welling up. The image is of a craftsman overtaken by his subject.

Verse 2 uses a doubled form for 'most handsome', a repeated syllable that intensifies the adjective. The Hebrew reads as something like 'you are fairer, fairest, among the sons of men'. The next line, 'grace has anointed your lips', uses a verb of pouring, and suggests that the king's words are as attractive as his face. The verse thus praises speech before it praises battle.

Verse 6 is the well-known verse. The word for God is elohim, and the phrase is 'Your throne, O God', with the vocative most naturally read as address. The verb 'endures' is not in the Hebrew, which reads 'Your throne, God, forever and ever', so the translator supplies it. Verse 7 then uses the same word twice: 'therefore God, your God, has anointed you'. The change from 'O God' to 'God, your God' marks a distinction between the one addressed and the one who anoints him. Hebrews 1:8-9 keeps both, and uses them to show the Son as God who has a God.

The scepter in verse 6 is described as a scepter of 'justice', a word that also means straightness. The king's rule is a straight rod, and its being straight is what makes it safe. In verse 4 the phrase 'truth and humility and justice' gathers three qualities that rarely appear together in a warrior. Humility in a conqueror is a startling word.

Finally, the 'daughter of Tyre' in verse 12 may be the bride herself or a group of visitors, since the Hebrew idiom for a city's population is 'daughter'. That ambiguity is worth admitting rather than resolving.

typology.type: The king whose throne endures forever, verses 6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The Davidic king with an eternal throne and a righteous scepter finds his fulfilment in Christ. Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes the verses as the Father's address to the Son, who is greater than the angels, and Isaiah 9:6-7 promises a child called Mighty God who will reign on David's throne with justice and righteousness forever. Luke records the angel's word to Mary that her son will be given the throne of His father David and that His kingdom will have no end, Luke 1:32-33. The escalation is from a dynasty that ended in exile to a king who never dies. The type falls short at the point of character: David's sons loved righteousness only partly, while Christ loved it perfectly.

typology.type: The anointing with the oil of joy above his companions, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The king is anointed beyond all his fellows. Hebrews 1:9 quotes the verse of the Son, and the claim is that no other, whether angel or man, shares His anointing. Jesus was anointed with the Holy Spirit at His baptism, Luke 3:22, and He read Isaiah 61 in Nazareth, the passage that speaks of the oil of joy, Luke 4:18-21. His people are anointed in Him, 2 Corinthians 1:21, but only as companions, never as equals. The type is limited because the earthly king's anointing was with oil, while Christ's was with the Spirit without measure, John 3:34.

typology.type: The bride who forgets her father's house, verses 10 to 15
typology.fulfillment: The bride called to leave her people and give herself to the king is a picture of the church. Paul says that Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, to present her to Himself as glorious, without stain or wrinkle, Ephesians 5:25-27. Revelation shows the bride arrayed in fine linen, bright and pure, Revelation 19:7-8, and the new Jerusalem prepared as a bride, Revelation 21:2. The correspondence escalates because the bridegroom pays the price for the bride's beauty, whereas the earthly king only receives it. It falls short in that the psalm's bride is an individual princess, while the church is a people from every nation.

typology.type: The king as warrior for truth and justice, verses 3 to 5
typology.fulfillment: The king rides out in splendour on behalf of truth, humility and justice, and his enemies fall. Revelation 19:11-16 shows the rider on the white horse, called Faithful and True, who judges and makes war in righteousness, and who bears the name KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS. In the meantime the victory is already won at the cross, where the powers were disarmed, Colossians 2:15. The type is limited by its violence; the New Testament sees the sword as coming from His mouth, Revelation 19:15, and His first coming as one of meekness, Matthew 21:5.

study.christ:
The psalm's connection to Christ is as clear as any in the Psalter, because the New Testament says so in so many words. Hebrews 1 opens with a claim that God has spoken finally through His Son, and then builds a case with quotations from the Psalms and other writings. At verse 8 the writer says, 'But about the Son He says: Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom.' That is the quotation of Psalm 45:6, and the next verse continues into 45:7. The Father is addressing the Son as God, and the Son is a king whose throne is eternal. The writer's point in the chapter is that the Son is not a created messenger but the radiance of God's glory, and Psalm 45 gives the Old Testament voice for that.

The quotation is not a stray proof text. It rests on the line of royal psalms and on the Davidic promise. If Psalm 2 says that the Lord's king is His Son and Psalm 110 says that the king sits at God's right hand, Psalm 45 adds that the king's throne is God's throne, and that his rule is a straight rod of justice. The picture that emerges is of a king who shares in God's own reign. In Christ it is realised: He was exalted to the highest place and given the name above every name, Philippians 2:9, and He is called KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS, Revelation 19:16.

The psalm's second half meets Christ in the figure of the bridegroom. John the Baptist says, 'The bride belongs to the bridegroom', John 3:29, and Jesus speaks of Himself as the bridegroom in Mark 2:19. Paul draws out the pattern in Ephesians 5, where Christ loves the church and gives Himself up for her to make her holy. The psalm's bride is told to bow to her lord, and in the New Testament the church is called to honour Christ, but the bridegroom is the one who first gave himself. The wedding of Psalm 45 anticipates the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7-9.

The verses about anointing add a personal note. The king is anointed with the oil of joy because he loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Hebrews 1:9 says the same of Christ, whose love of righteousness is the ground of His exaltation. The New Testament teaches that He learned obedience through what He suffered and was then crowned, Hebrews 5:8-9, so that His joy is the joy of a finished work.

A note of restraint: the psalm's details of ivory palaces and myrrh are not each a coded reference to Christ. The New Testament's warrant is the central claim about the throne and anointing, and the marriage image, and it is enough.
study.god:
The psalm tells us first that God is the source of the king's blessing: 'God has blessed you forever', verse 2. Nothing in the king's beauty or victories is presented as his own achievement. The gracious lips and the anointing are God's gifts. In verse 7, the anointing is done by 'God, your God', and the phrase shows that even the highest human king has a God above him.

Second, God is a lover of righteousness. The king is praised for loving what God loves and hating what God hates, and it is because of that character that he is anointed. The psalm therefore reveals God's own moral nature. A God who honours a king for hating wickedness is a God who will not be mocked by evil, and the throne He establishes has justice as its scepter. Psalm 89:14 says that righteousness and justice are the foundation of God's own throne, and Psalm 45 shows that foundation carried out in the reign of His king.

Third, God is the God of covenant promise. The poet's final lines promise sons who will succeed their fathers and a name remembered through all generations. Behind that lies the promise of 2 Samuel 7 that God would establish David's house. The psalm therefore shows God as faithful across time and as a giver of joy to His people through the king.

Fourth, the psalm holds a question about God's identity that the New Testament answers. The king is addressed as 'God', and he is anointed by 'God, your God'. If the Son is God and has a God, then God is not solitary, and there is a relationship within His life of love and anointing. Hebrews uses the verse to show the deity of the Son without denying the Father, and the church later found in such texts the material for its doctrine of the Trinity. The psalm does not explain that doctrine. It supplies a strange and beautiful hint.

For worship, the psalm makes praise an art. The poet gives his best skill to his subject, and his heart is stirred. The church can learn from this that worship should be careful, joyful and full of wonder at the beauty of the king, and that the God who gives such a king deserves the praise of every generation.

crossReferences.note: The Father says to the Son, 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever', quoting Psalm 45:6-7 in full. The writer uses the psalm to show that the Son is not an angel but the eternal king who is himself addressed as God, and whose anointing is above all his companions.

A child is born who will be called Mighty God and who will reign on David's throne with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore. It matches Psalm 45:6-7 in the double claim of divine title and unending righteous rule, and shows that the Old Testament already spoke of the Davidic king in these terms.

The Lord installs His king on Zion and calls him His Son. Psalm 45 shows that same king at his wedding, and Hebrews 1:5 quotes Psalm 2 just before Psalm 45. The two psalms together give the king's sonship and his throne.

The Lord says to David's Lord, 'Sit at My right hand.' It presents the king as sharing God's authority, which is the same idea that Psalm 45:6 expresses by calling his throne eternal. Jesus used this psalm to show that the Messiah is more than a son of David.

The prayer that God would endow the king with His justice and righteousness, so that he judges the afflicted rightly. It is the request that Psalm 45:4 and 45:6 celebrate as granted: a king who rides for justice and whose scepter is justice.

The anointed one gives 'the oil of joy for mourning' to those who grieve. It uses the same phrase as Psalm 45:7 and shows the Messiah's anointing as a gift to others. Jesus read the opening of this chapter at Nazareth and said it was fulfilled that day, Luke 4:18-21.

Solomon's foreign wives turned his heart after other gods. The counsel to the bride in Psalm 45:10 to forget her people and belong wholly to the king becomes a warning when read beside this: the earthly king's own loyalty failed, which is why a greater king is needed.

John the Baptist says the bride belongs to the bridegroom and that he is only the friend who rejoices to hear the bridegroom's voice. He identifies Jesus as the bridegroom of Psalm 45 and the prophets, and he shows that the joy of the wedding has arrived.

Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her to present her as glorious, holy and blameless. It fills in the psalm's wedding picture: the bride's beauty in Psalm 45:13 is what the bridegroom's sacrifice produces.

The marriage of the Lamb has come and His bride has made herself ready, clothed in fine linen. The wedding procession of Psalm 45:14-15 reaches its goal here, with the joyful company led into the presence of the king.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 45 belongs to the middle of the Bible's story, where the promise of a king is held in a real royal court and pointed toward a fuller hope. The story begins with human beings made to rule under God, Genesis 1:26-28, and it falters when they fall. From Abraham on, God promises kings, Genesis 17:6, and Jacob's blessing gives Judah the scepter, Genesis 49:10. The promise narrows to David, and 2 Samuel 7:12-16 assures him of a son whose throne will be established forever. Psalm 45 is the song of a court that believed that promise and wanted to see it in a wedding.

The story then shows how the promise was tested. Solomon began well and ended in idolatry, 1 Kings 11:1-4. The kings that followed were mostly worse, and the dynasty ended in exile. The psalm's picture of a righteous, victorious and joyful king was never fully seen in any of them. The prophets kept it alive: Isaiah expects a child who will be Mighty God on David's throne, Isaiah 9:6-7, and Jeremiah expects a righteous Branch, Jeremiah 23:5-6.

The New Testament announces that the king has come. The angel tells Mary that her son will receive the throne of David, Luke 1:32-33. Hebrews opens with the Son addressed in the words of Psalm 45. The bride image, which the prophets used for God and Israel, is now used of Christ and the church, and the church is being prepared for the wedding, Ephesians 5:25-27.

The story ends in the wedding itself. Revelation 19:7-9 announces the marriage of the Lamb, and Revelation 21:2 shows the holy city coming down as a bride adorned for her husband. The king's name is remembered through all generations, as the psalm promised, and the nations praise him, Revelation 21:24 and 7:9-10. The wedding song is sung at last by a people who have been made ready by the groom himself. The dynasty that seemed to end in exile continues in the Son of David whose throne has no end, and the poet's promise, 'the nations will praise you forever and ever', is fulfilled.

quiz.q: What does the poet compare his own tongue to in verse 1?

options.text: The pen of a skillful writer.
options.note: The poet describes his inspired composition using the image of a skilled scribe's pen.

options.text: A sharpened sword.
options.note: The sword imagery belongs to the king in verse 3, not to the poet's tongue.

options.text: A harp played in the palace.
options.note: Harps appear later, verse 8, describing the king's palace, not the poet's own tongue.

options.text: A trumpet announcing victory.
options.note: No trumpet appears in this psalm; the specific image for the poet's tongue is a skillful writer's pen.

quiz.q: What is the king summoned to do in verses 3-5?

options.text: Strap on his sword and ride forth in majesty and victory for truth and justice.
options.note: The king is called as a mighty warrior to ride out triumphantly on behalf of truth, humility, and justice.

options.text: Lay down his weapons and seek peace with all nations.
options.note: The text calls him to arm himself and ride forth in victory, not to disarm.

options.text: Retreat to his palace and avoid conflict.
options.note: The summons is to active, victorious battle, not retreat.

options.text: Send his armies ahead while he remains behind.
options.note: The king himself is called to ride forth personally in splendor and victory.

quiz.q: How does verse 6 address the king's throne, language later quoted in Hebrews 1:8-9?

options.text: "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever."
options.note: This direct address of the throne as God's own is quoted by Hebrews as the Father's words to the Son.

options.text: "Your throne will one day pass to your enemies."
options.note: The verse promises the throne endures forever, the opposite of passing to enemies.

options.text: "Your throne is like the thrones of other kings."
options.note: The verse's point is precisely that this throne is unlike other kings' thrones, called God's own.

options.text: "Your throne will be established by your armies."
options.note: The text credits God, not military strength, with establishing and sustaining the throne forever.

quiz.q: According to verses 10-11, what is the bride called to do?

options.text: Forget her people and father's house, and incline her ear to the king.
options.note: She is called to undivided devotion to the king, forsaking her former household loyalty.

options.text: Return quickly to her own family and homeland.
options.note: The text calls her to forget, not return to, her people and father's house.

options.text: Remain equally loyal to both her family and the king.
options.note: The summons is to singular devotion to the king, not divided loyalty.

options.text: Bring her own army to help the king in battle.
options.note: The bride's calling here is devotion and honor to the king, not military assistance.

quiz.q: What does the New Testament book of Hebrews do with Psalm 45:6-7?

options.text: It quotes the verses as words the Father speaks to the Son, proof of Christ's deity and eternal throne.
options.note: Hebrews 1:8-9 applies this royal wedding language directly to Christ as evidence of His full divinity.

options.text: It dismisses the verses as merely poetic exaggeration about a human king.
options.note: Hebrews treats the verses with full theological seriousness as address to the Son, not as mere exaggeration.

options.text: It applies the verses only to angels, not to Christ.
options.note: Hebrews 1 actually contrasts Christ with the angels, applying this psalm's throne language to the Son specifically.

options.text: It reinterprets the verses as referring to the future church, not any king.
options.note: Hebrews applies the verses to Christ the King Himself, not directly to the church as its referent.

questions: This wedding song describes a king whose righteousness, victory, and splendor exceed any mere human ruler. What does it stir in you to know that Christ, the true King this psalm ultimately describes, reigns in perfect righteousness forever?

The bride is called to forget her people and father's house for undivided devotion to the king. What lesser loyalties competes most for the devotion Christ, your true Bridegroom, calls you to give Him alone?
Hebrews quotes this psalm as the Father's own address to the Son, calling Him God. How does meditating on Christ's full deity change the way you approach Him in prayer and worship?

The king is praised for loving righteousness and hating wickedness, verse 7. Where in your life is this pattern, love for what is right and hatred for what is wrong, weakest right now, and what would it look like to grow in it?
This psalm anticipates the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19. How does picturing the church as Christ's beloved, honored bride shape how you see your own place in His story?

translationNotes.note: My heart is stirred renders a Hebrew verb picturing a bubbling over or overflowing, describing the poet's inspiration pouring out into composed verse.
Your throne, O God has been read either as a direct vocative address to the king as God, or as a description, your divine throne; Hebrews 1:8 reads it as direct address, applying it to the Son.
The gold of Ophir was proverbial in Scripture for the finest, most valuable gold, 1 Kings 9:28, underscoring the queen's supreme honor at the king's right hand.
